query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new coupled computational framework that integrates self‐consistent ab initio electron–phonon coupling with machine‐learned anharmonic lattice dynamics will separately and accurately predict the lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr. This approach should achieve roughly a 25–30% improvement in predictive accuracy over traditional Debye‐temperature‐based and force constant variation models by correctly capturing local disorder, anharmonic effects, and impurity (e.g., 1 wt.% oxygen) scattering.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr alloy in both (a) an ideal, defect‐free bulk state and (b) a state with minor impurity contamination (approximately 1 wt.% oxygen).
generation.intervention: Implement a computational model that couples self‐consistent ab initio methods for electron–phonon interactions with machine‐learned interatomic potentials to compute advanced anharmonic lattice dynamics. This framework explicitly treats local atomic disorder and scattering effects independently for electrons and phonons.
generation.conditions: Temperature regimes covering both low temperatures (<200 K), where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable, and high temperatures (300–1200 K) where total conductivity measurements of 10–17 W/(K m) have been experimentally reported. The model should be applied to specimens representing both pure and 1 wt.% oxygen‐contaminated states.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic-scale disorder and anharmonic variations in interatomic force constants, including impurity-induced scattering effects.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced capture of electron–phonon coupling effects through ab initio evaluations combined with ML-driven lattice dynamical corrections to account for anharmonic phonon scattering and local disorder. This decoupling allows separate predictions of electronic and lattice conductivity channels rather than relying on averaged Debye or defect-free approximations.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will separately predict lattice and electronic contributions that (a) are nearly equal below 200 K and (b) combine to yield total thermal conductivities in the 10–17 W/(K m) range at high temperatures (300–1200 K). Improvements should be observable as a 25–30% reduction in the deviation from experimental measurements compared with earlier approaches.
generation.baseline: Existing approaches based on DFT‐derived elastic properties and simplified lattice dynamics (e.g., Debye approximations) that do not decouple the heat transport channels or capture impurity effects.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy HfNbTaTiZr alloys under near-equilibrium conditions for both defect‐free and minor impurity states. Its validity beyond slight oxygen contamination or under extreme non-equilibrium conditions remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: The full decoupling of electron and phonon contributions in environments with severe disorder or under extreme thermal gradients may introduce uncertainties. Furthermore, the exact magnitude of the improvement might vary with the detailed treatment of anharmonicity and impurity scattering.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled purity (defect‐free) and with 1 wt.% oxygen. Use thermal transport experiments (e.g., laser flash analysis, time-domain thermoreflectance) combined with techniques that can decouple electronic and lattice contributions (e.g., Seebeck coefficient measurements, frequency‐resolved thermal conductivity) over a temperature range spanning below 200 K and 300–1200 K.
measurements: Separate quantification of lattice (phonon) and electronic thermal conductivities across the specified temperature ranges
Total thermal conductivity measurements for direct comparison with predicted combined values
Assessment of impurity-induced modifications at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured separate contributions (lattice and electronic) do not match the model's decoupled predictions within a 30% margin of error, or if the temperature dependence of the separate contributions deviates significantly from the predicted trends (i.e., comparable contributions below 200 K and proper total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures), then the hypothesis is falsified.

3D Ink‐Extrusion Printing

The 3D ink extrusion printing, sintering, and silicide coating processes are shown in Figure 1 a . The ≈410 µm filaments containing metallic/hydride powders are printed layer by layer to produce complex parts, including a lattice sandwich structure, as shown in Figure 1b . When the filaments are extruded, the solvent (dichloromethane, DCM) evaporates near‐instantaneously, and the binder (polystyrene, PS) precipitates, leading to a quick increase in the strength of filaments that helps the structure to self‐support. After sintering, these samples are nearly fully densified and show neither cracking nor warpage. After a subsequent silicide coating, the oxidation resistance of the 3D‐printed part is very significantly improved, which is a key step to making 3D‐printed RHEA structures useful at high temperatures.

This trend is particularly important for multi-component alloys, because the ordering can drive the system to various microstructural states, such as crystalline or intermetallic solids, from the disordered FCC ( A1 ), BCC ( A2 ), or HCP ( A3 ) conditions. In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems [24] , [44] – [46] . decision.trend: Early predictive approaches focused on analytical estimates by varying atomic masses and force constants and using DFT‐derived elastic properties, all under the assumption of perfect, defect‐free bulk crystals. These methods incorporated simplified parameters (e.g., the Debye temperature) to approximate lattice heat transport and often lumped lattice and electronic contributions together. In contrast, experimental studies on HfNbTaTiZr show that below 200 K the lattice and electronic channels are comparable and at high temperatures (300–1200 K) even low levels of impurities (e.g., 1 wt.% oxygen) have a measurable effect on total conductivity. Although these earlier methods provided rough estimates of total thermal conductivity, none successfully decoupled the lattice and electronic contributions while accounting for the full atomic‐scale complexity and disorder present in real materials.
decision.unsolved: No current model quantitatively and separately predicts lattice and electronic thermal conductivities for HfNbTaTiZr across the wide temperature range and impurity states. In particular, existing methods cannot capture the scattering and anharmonic effects arising from complex local environments, nor can they benchmark predictions against the separate experimental signatures occurring at low (<200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperatures.
decision.lever: Develop a coupled, atomistically informed computational framework that integrates self-consistent ab initio evaluations of electron-phonon coupling with advanced anharmonic lattice dynamics computed via machine-learned interatomic potentials. This approach should explicitly treat the local atomic disorder, incorporate corrections for impurity effects, and decouple the electron and phonon contributions to thermal conductivity.
decision.why: Such a framework naturally extends previous DFT and force-constant variation studies by going beyond ideal, defect-free approximations. By leveraging machine learning to capture local variations and anharmonic effects, the method is expected to achieve around a 25–30% improvement in predictive accuracy compared to analytical approximations. Its predictions can be directly compared with measured total conductivities (10–17 W/(K m)) over high temperatures and with the balance of lattice vs electronic contributions observed experimentally at low temperatures, thereby providing decisive benchmarks that would falsify the model if the predicted separate contributions do not align with the experimental trends in both pure and oxygen-contaminated specimens.
